key_insight: During brief handgrip exercise, muscle oxygen saturation fell less in mitochondrial disease but more in sarcopenia than in their respective comparison groups.
clinical_relevance: These contrasting oxygenation patterns suggest NIRS could help characterize muscle dysfunction, but diagnostic usefulness remains unproven.
method: Compared 10 adults with genetically confirmed mitochondrial disease with 19 matched controls.
Assessed 23 older adults, including 7 with probable or confirmed sarcopenia.
Recorded force and NIRS during 3 minutes of intermittent handgrip exercise at 40% maximal voluntary contraction.
evidence_signal: Late-exercise tissue saturation responses differed for mitochondrial disease versus controls (p=0.02) and sarcopenia versus non-sarcopenia (p=0.05), while total haemoglobin responses were similar.
watch_item: Small samples, including only seven sarcopenia cases, limit generalizability; this study concerns muscle physiology, not AI cancer drug discovery.
paper_title: Near infrared spectroscopy during non-ischaemic handgrip exercise reveals divergent muscle oxygenation signatures in mitochondrial disease and sarcopenia
